A peek at something we've built in-house at @Vizz Ads.

For every client, we track what their competitors are running on Meta. Every live ad, grouped by idea, sorted by format, hook and offer.

This one (brand anonymised) took about five minutes to read and told us:

→ Their competitor is running far more video than static
→ The same three hooks show up again and again
→ They've quietly been leaning on discount offers

That's a creative brief, written by the market.

Most ad partners check competitors once, at the pitch, and never again. Day-to-day account work always wins over "we'll look at that later".

So we built it to run without anyone having to remember.

What do you check about your competitors, and how often?

5 things we check in a new ad account before looking at a single campaign.

Any founder can run these in an afternoon.

1. Is tracking telling the truth?

Place one real test order and trace it through every platform. If the numbers don't match, nothing else matters yet.

2. What does the business actually need?

ROAS, new customers or profit. Agree one before touching anything. Otherwise the account chases a number nobody chose.

3. Is the structure fighting the algorithm?

Too many campaigns and ad sets split the budget so thin that nothing gets enough data to learn. Fewer, bigger ad sets learn faster.

4. How old is the creative?

If your best ad is six months old, new ones are overdue. Fresh creative is often the cheapest fix in the account.

5. Who is it really reaching?

Great ROAS can just be people who would have bought anyway. Check new vs returning customers, not just ROAS.

Which one would worry you most?

Eight months ago I went independent and started @Vizz Ads.

A few honest lessons so far:

1. Running ads is the easy part.
After 13 years, the work itself felt familiar from day one. Finding the right clients is the real job.

2. Saying no is a skill.
Some briefs weren't the right fit. Turning them down early saved everyone time.

3. Being small is an advantage.
Clients get the person who actually does the work. No handoffs, no juniors, no waiting.

4. Building in public feels uncomfortable.
Posting here still doesn't come naturally. But every conversation that's started from a post has been worth it.

5. The network you built before matters more than you think.
Thank you to everyone who's reached out, referred someone, or just cheered from the sidelines.

Still early. Still learning. Grateful for all of it.

Black Friday is four weeks away. Most brands will start planning their ads in three.

What wins Black Friday happens now, not in November. Here's what we're doing with @Vizz Ads clients this week:

→ Test your creative now
You need proven ads going in, not untested ones. Launch new concepts now so you know your winners before costs spike.

→ Build your warm audiences
Ad costs climb sharply in late November. People who've already engaged with you are far cheaper to convert. Spend now to fill those pools.

→ Fix tracking before the rush
If something breaks on the busiest weekend of the year, you're flying blind with your biggest budget.

→ Agree the offer early
Last-minute discount decisions mean last-minute creative, which means rushed ads.

→ Plan beyond the weekend
Cyber Monday and the December gifting window often beat Black Friday itself for considered purchases.

The brands that look calm on the day did the work in October.

Where are you up to?

posts.linkedin_text:
Regulated doesn't have to mean boring.

At @Vizz Ads we run Meta and Google ads for an FCA-regulated investment platform. Working in a regulated category has sharpened how we brief, write and build every ad.

Three things it's taught us:

→ Compliance is a brief, not a blocker
Knowing the rules before the first idea, not after the first draft, leads to better ideas and fewer rewrites.

→ Specific beats bold
You can't promise returns. So the ads win on real detail and plain words, which tends to persuade better anyway.

→ Build the warning in, never bolt it on
The risk warning comes from an approved template on every asset. One less thing to get wrong at speed.

If you're in finance, health or any category with rules, good ads are still on the table.

What's the hardest rule you work around?

posts.linkedin_text:
Nobody hires an interior designer from an ad alone.

At @Vizz Ads we run Meta lead ads for Anyon, a premium interior design studio. For a service like this, the sale starts with a conversation, so the ads are built to start one:

→ Offer a consultation
Invite homeowners to talk to a designer about their project. The first step feels smaller and safer than a hard sell.

→ Keep the form short
A few simple questions, so the design team can follow up quickly and personally.

→ Speak to who's hiring
Homeowners, designers and decorators hire for different reasons. Speak to each one.

If your service needs a chat before a sale, your ads should start that chat.

What does the first conversation look like for your customers?
